extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, and researchers interested in peer review quality and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journals and researchers on evaluating the quality, validity, and reliability of peer review reports and peer review processes, including practical recommendations for structuring reviews, collecting feedback, and publishing metrics. Aimed at helping editorial teams decide which aspects of their peer review workflows are working and which need improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and reliability of peer review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the validity and reliability of peer review reports to determine which aspects of journal peer review processes are working well and which are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EASE draft guidelines provide a high-level framework for evaluating validity and reliability. The aim is to help journals gain a better understanding of what’s working in their peer review and what isn’t, acknowledging inherent complexity and variability across disciplines and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder rating of review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite authors, editors, and reviewers to rate review reports to capture perceptions of review quality from multiple stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The draft recommends asking these groups to rate review reports so journals can understand how everyone perceives the peer review process. Note the interview caution that authors/readers may not be comfortable giving simple 1–5 ratings once they understand complexity; ratings should be used as an initial proxy and conversation starter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured peer reviews (defined review questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require structured peer reviews by clearly defining the specific questions reviewers should answer rather than leaving evaluations implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘We often assume if a reviewer hasn’t commented on something, it means they are okay with it. But that needs to be explicitly stated for it to be true.’ Example: force reviewers to state whether they stand behind the statistics, which reveals when additional expertise is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit assessment of methods, limitations, and data validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reviewers explicitly evaluate the soundness of methods, possible limitations of the study, and the validity of the data presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured prompts should ask reviewers about methods, limitations, and data validity so that gaps are more likely to be flagged (e.g., reviewers indicating 'my expertise isn’t in this area' or 'needs another set of eyes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Component-based quality dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider dividing peer review quality into multiple components (e.g., good language, good reporting) rather than treating it as a single undifferentiated measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidelines suggest quality could be separated into components such as reporting quality, language, and other aspects. This supports more nuanced evaluation than a single overall score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simple rating scales as an initial proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple scales (for example, 1–5 stars) as an initial proxy metric for review quality, recognizing their limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview notes: '1-5 stars is an initial proxy for something very complex, and let us use it as a jumping-off point.' Simple scales can provide baseline, but require follow-up discussion and possible decomposition into subcomponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine collection and publication of satisfaction/quality metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect routine data on author, reviewer, and editorial satisfaction (e.g., surveys) and consider publishing these metrics to track and benchmark performance over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interview compares this to universities publishing yearly student satisfaction surveys. Journals rarely publish such routine metrics; doing so could provide baseline data to inform improvements and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about checks performed (‘nutrition labels’ for articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about what checks the journal performed during peer review so readers can understand what 'quality peer review' entailed for a published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed idea: something akin to nutrition labels for academic articles that state which checks were performed (e.g., statistical review, data availability checks). Makes clear what work the journal did vs. what it did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect reviewer role limits — do not expect data forensics
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that peer reviewers are not expected to perform specialized data forensics or detect well-concealed data fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interview emphasizes that data forensics is a different field requiring expertise; peer reviewers typically check soundness of reporting and argument based on presented data, and should not be tasked with deep forensic investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure appropriate expertise and sufficient number of reviewers (consensus-based verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Match reviewer expertise to the manuscript and consider the number of reviewers: consensus among multiple experts increases confidence in assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional peer review uses two to three reviewers; involving more experts could better classify agreement on issues. Quality also depends on the initial submission quality and reviewer expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge complexity and handle trade-offs in scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize trade-offs when scoring reviews (e.g., a review that is excellent overall but misses a significant problem) and be cautious about how single omissions affect overall quality scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interview notes difficulty in defining how much a missed significant problem should reduce an overall score. Existing tools/questionnaires for scoring reviews have not become standard because of these challenges; any scoring system must account for such nuances.
